Section 1 describes the PBH background and the resulting ALP distribution, Section 2 the treatment of ALP decays, Section 3 how each constraint is implemented, and Section 4 the X-ray bound. 1. PBH BACKGROUND AND THE ALP DISTRIBUTION A. Assumptions Throughout we work in natural units with G = M−2 Pl and normalize the scale factor so that a0 = 1. For the late-time cosmology we adopt the Planck 2018 parameters [30]. We take all PBHs to have the same initial mass Mi and to be nonrotating, and we ignore accretion and mergers. This is a reasonable starting point, since PBHs that form from rare peaks during radiation domination are expected to be born with small spins [31, 32]. A nonzero spin, or a spread in the initial masses, would modify both the evaporation rate and the spectrum of the emitted particles [33–35], and we do not consider these cases here. The SM particles produced by evaporation thermalize by the time the PBHs disappear [3], whereas the ALPs interact only through their decay into photons. Our results therefore apply only where plasma effects can neither thermalize nor reabsorb the ALPs. We also treat the production and the decay of the ALPs as two separate stages. For this to be valid, decays during evaporation have to be negligible, which requires ΓaτBH ≪ 1. In practice this condition is conservative, because the ALPs are relativistic when they are emitted and time dilation only slows down their decay.
